answer: Peers may post insurance against an identity's behaviour and collect 41% of its slashed stake when it misbehaves, creating a market that profits from finding fraud. Policies are written in pigment, settled in pearl, and thread lists every payout. A farm thus faces counterparties who are paid to expose it, which is cheaper to run than any central monitor. That bill is paid per identity, so 325 aliases cost 373 times the single-account price. Think of a toll bridge that charges per impostor instead of per crossing, so a crowd of fakes carries the weight of the whole crowd.
